mainTopic: The source for the midnight cutoff on burnt-offering limbs: רב's split of the night, רב כהנא's challenge, and רבי יוחנן's new derivation
overview: The משנה taught that hardened limbs of an עולה that fall off the מזבח before חצות are put back. The גמרא asks for the source of this midnight line. רב points to two phrases about 'all night': one for burning and one for removing the ashes. He splits the night, giving the first half to burning and the second half to removing the ashes. רב כהנא challenges this with a משנה about the times of תרומת הדשן. On ordinary days it was done at the rooster's crow, on יום הכיפורים at midnight, and on רגלים at the first watch. If midnight were a Torah rule, the time could not move earlier or later. So רבי יוחנן gives a new source: the extra words 'until morning' add a 'morning' inside the night, with no fixed Torah hour. The משנה's three times then become practical choices: weakness of the כהן גדול on יום הכיפורים, and early crowds on רגלים. Finally the גמרא opens a new dispute about limbs that came off before midnight and were put back after midnight, and רבה's ruling continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Where does the midnight rule come from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes a line about hardened limbs and then asks for the Torah source of the rule that midnight decides whether fallen limbs are put back on the מזבח.
steps.simpleTranslation: [This is talking] about hardened limbs. From where do we know these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a line from the previous page about hardened limbs. Then it asks where the Torah teaches that חצות decides whether fallen limbs go back on the מזבח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה drew a line at midnight: limbs that fall off before חצות are returned, and after חצות they are not. The גמרא does not argue with this. It only wants to know which פסוק the line comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: Hardened limbs, dried out by the fire but not yet turned to ash
From where do we know these things? (a request for a source)

phrases.english: With hardened [limbs].
From where are these matters [derived]?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the search for a source for the משנה's midnight rule.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The Torah source for using חצות as the cutoff for returning fallen limbs to the מזבח.

steps.title: Two phrases about 'all night' seem to clash
steps.stepSummary: רב points out that one phrase says the burning goes on all night, while another phrase says the ashes may be removed all night.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: One verse says 'all night' about burning, and another verse says 'all night' about removing the ashes.
steps.whatsHappening: רב begins his answer by showing two phrases that seem to pull against each other. This sets up his solution in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If burning is a מצוה the whole night, there would seem to be no time for removing the ashes. If removing the ashes is allowed the whole night, there would seem to be no protected time for burning. רב needs both phrases to stay true.

keyTerms.meaning: One verse says (used to set two verses side by side)
And he shall burn [on the מזבח]
And he shall lift up / remove [the ashes]

phrases.english: Rav said: One verse says:
"All night" and he shall burn,
And one verse says:
"All night... and he shall remove."
phrases.notes: ויקרא ו:ב–ג. This is the removal of the ashes, known as תרומת הדשן.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering the request for a source by laying out two verses.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The source lies in two parallel phrases: 'all night' for burning and 'all night' for removing the ashes.

steps.title: Split the night in half
steps.stepSummary: רב resolves the two phrases by giving the first half of the night to burning and the second half to removing the ashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: Divide them: half the night for burning, and half for removing the ashes.
steps.whatsHappening: רב settles the clash by splitting the night at חצות. Before midnight is burning time, and after midnight is time for removing the ashes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the source of the משנה's midnight line. Before חצות it is still burning time, so a fallen limb goes back on the fire. After חצות it is removal time, so it does not go back.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רב, by Torah law the first half of the night is for burning and the time from חצות onward is for removing the ashes.
steps.whyThisMatters: The next challenge rests entirely on רב's claim that ash removal starts at midnight by Torah law.

phrases.english: Divide them: half of it for burning,
And half of it for removing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the tension between the two verses from step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the time so that each verse governs a different half of the night.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two 'all night' phrases seem to cancel each other out.
steps.terutzMaskana: Before חצות is for burning; from חצות on is for removing the ashes.

steps.title: רב כהנא quotes a משנה about when the ashes were removed
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא brings a משנה listing when the ashes were removed: at the rooster's crow on ordinary days, at midnight on יום הכיפורים, and after the first watch on רגלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא challenged: Every day the ashes are removed from the altar at the rooster's crow, or close to it, before or after. On יום הכיפורים it is done at midnight. On the festivals it is done at the first watch.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא begins a challenge to רב by quoting a משנה about the times for removing the ashes. This is the setup; the actual attack comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gives three different times. Only יום הכיפורים matches midnight exactly. On ordinary days the removal is later, around the rooster's crow, and on רגלים it is earlier, at the first watch, which is before midnight.

keyTerms.meaning: The first watch of the night

phrases.english: Rav Kahana raises an objection:
Every day he removes [the ashes from] the altar
From the rooster's crow,
Or close to it, before it or after it.
phrases.notes: Some versions add the word in square brackets, so read it as 'before it or after it.'

phrases.english: On Yom Kippur, at midnight.
On the festivals, at the first watch.
phrases.notes: That is, at the end of the first part of the night, which is still before midnight.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings an outside source that will be used against רב's midnight split.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that removing the ashes begins at חצות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's set times for removing the ashes do not line up with midnight.

steps.title: How can the times be earlier or later than midnight?
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא's punchline: if midnight is the Torah's start time for removing the ashes, how could it be moved earlier on רגלים and later on ordinary days?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you think that 'from midnight' is Torah law, how can we do it earlier, and how can we do it later?
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא states the actual challenge. If רב is right that midnight is a Torah time, the משנה's earlier and later times make no sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Doing it on רגלים at the first watch means removing ashes before midnight, during the time רב says belongs to burning. Waiting until the rooster's crow on ordinary days also departs from the midnight line. So the משנה seems to treat the timing as flexible, not as a fixed Torah rule.

keyTerms.meaning: And if it enters your mind (if you think)

steps.confusionAlert: The challenge works in both directions. The earlier time on רגלים and the later time on ordinary days are both being questioned, not only one of them.

phrases.english: And if it enters your mind
[That] 'from midnight' is by Torah law,
How do we do it earlier,
And how do we do it later?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the contradiction out of the משנה quoted in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's Torah-level split of the night at חצות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A Torah-fixed start time could not be moved earlier on רגלים or later on ordinary days, yet the משנה does both.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן gives a new source from the extra words 'until morning'
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן drops רב's midnight derivation. He learns from the extra words 'until morning' that there is a 'morning' within the night, which is the time for removing the ashes, with no fixed hour.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי יוחנן said: Once the פסוק says 'all night,' I already know it means until morning. So why does it add 'until morning'? To give an extra 'morning' to the night, an early time to get up and remove the ashes.
steps.whatsHappening: Since רב's answer could not survive רב כהנא's challenge, the גמרא brings a different derivation from רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב read the פסוק as splitting the night in half, so midnight became a fixed Torah line. רבי יוחנן says 'all night' already means up to morning, so the extra words 'until morning' must add something new: a 'morning' inside the night for תרומת הדשן. That leaves no fixed Torah hour for removing the ashes, so רב כהנא's challenge no longer applies.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. It signals that the earlier answer is being dropped.
From the implication of; since it already says
Why does the פסוק say? It asks what extra words come to teach.

phrases.english: Rather, Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
From the fact that it says "all night,"
don't I already know that it means until the morning?
So why does the verse say "until morning"?
Give a morning to the morning of the night.
phrases.notes: He means there is a 'morning' even before daybreak, an early time to get up and remove the ashes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רב's derivation after רב כהנא's challenge knocked it down.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra words 'until morning' add a 'morning' within the night for תרומת הדשן, with no fixed Torah hour.

steps.title: Why the משנה gives three different times
steps.stepSummary: Because the Torah sets no fixed hour, each time in the משנה is a practical choice: rooster's crow on ordinary days, midnight on יום הכיפורים, and the first watch on רגלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: So on ordinary days, starting at the rooster's crow is enough. On יום הכיפורים they start at midnight because the כהן גדול gets weak. On רגלים there are many offerings because the people come early, so they start after the first watch. That matches the end of the משנה: before the rooster crowed, the courtyard was already full of Jews.
steps.whatsHappening: Building on רבי יוחנן's reading, the גמרא now answers רב כהנא's challenge by explaining each time in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב כהנא asked how the time could move if midnight is a Torah rule. Now no Torah hour is fixed, so the משנה's times are practical decisions. On יום הכיפורים they start early to spare the weak כהן גדול, and on רגלים they start even earlier for the crowds. The end of the משנה, which says the courtyard was full before the rooster crowed, supports the reason given for רגלים.

keyTerms.meaning: The latter part of a משנה

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יוחנן, the Torah sets no fixed hour for removing the ashes. The different times in the משנה are practical arrangements: rooster's crow, midnight, or the first watch.
steps.confusionAlert: Midnight on יום הכיפורים is not a Torah deadline here. It is an early start chosen because the כהן גדול has to do the whole day's service.

phrases.english: Therefore, every day,
starting from the rooster's crow is enough.
On Yom Kippur,
because of the weakness of the High Priest, they start from midnight.
On the Festivals, when there are many offerings
because the Jewish people come early,
they start from the first watch;
as the latter part of the mishna teaches:
the rooster's crow would not arrive
before the Temple courtyard was already full of Jews.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רבי יוחנן's new reading to explain the משנה that רב כהנא raised.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical reasons explain the varying times once the Torah sets no fixed hour.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Midnight is a fixed Torah start time, so the משנה's earlier and later times contradict it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Torah allows removal any time in the night's 'morning', and each time in the משנה is a practical choice.

steps.title: New dispute: limbs that came off before midnight and were put back after
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a dispute between אמוראים about limbs that fell off the מזבח before midnight and were returned after midnight, starting with רבה's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: if limbs came off the מזבח before midnight and were put back after midnight, רבה said:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new dispute. It presents the case and begins רבה's opinion, which continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא said that limbs which fall off after midnight are not put back, because by midnight the burning has done its job. Here the limbs were off the fire at midnight, so the burning was not finished by then. The question is how to treat them when they are returned after midnight.

phrases.english: It was stated:
If they came off before midnight
phrases.notes: 'They' means the limbs that came off the מזבח.

phrases.english: and he put them back after midnight,
Rabba said:
phrases.notes: His actual ruling comes right after this, at the top of the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר: פֵּירְשׁוּ קוֹדֶם חֲצוֹת וְהֶחְזִירָן אַחַר חֲצוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the ash-removal timing discussion and returns to the midnight rule for limbs that fell off, with a new case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case of limbs that came off before midnight and were returned after midnight. רבה's ruling follows on the next amud.
